title: The payment lifecycle
subtitle: What really happens after the customer taps "Pay", and the states your code must track until the money is in your bank.

c.v: This is a made-up example, but each rule in it comes from processor docs.

Meera's team runs an online furniture shop in India. To avoid refunds for items that are out of stock, the shop takes card payments in two steps. At checkout it only places a hold on the card. When a sofa ships, a job captures the money.
In one busy month, some sofas shipped late, 9 or 10 days after checkout. The capture job logged "error" for those orders, and nobody read the log. The sofas went out anyway.
Their processor's rule was simple. For many online card payments, a hold lasts about 7 days. If you do not capture before it expires, the funds are released and the payment becomes canceled.
The shop gave away the sofas for free.

Nobody saw it for weeks. The order table said "paid" because the hold had worked. The team found it only at month end. The money in the bank was lower than the sum of "paid" orders, and finance asked why.
Three bugs, one
root cause
. The team treated a payment as one event, "paid". It is really a series of states over many days, and each state can fail.
A card payment has several parties.
Customer
: the person who pays with a card.
Merchant
: your business.
Payment processor
or gateway: a company such as Stripe or Adyen that your code talks to.
Acquiring bank
: processes card payments for merchants. It sends the authorization request to the customer's bank through the
card networks
Card network
: the network of a card brand, such as Visa or Mastercard.
Issuing bank
: the bank that gave the customer the card.
The payment then moves through states. Your code must track each one.
Authorization
: the issuing bank checks that funds are there and holds the amount.
Capture
: the money moves from the issuing bank toward you.
Settlement
: the customer's bank transfers the funds to the processor. Adyen marks a payment Settled at this point.
Payout
: the processor sends money from your available balance to your bank account.
The key idea.
"Paid" is not one moment. A payment is a state machine that runs for days. Store each state, learn about changes from verified webhooks, and check the final money against the processor's report.
Step through one ₹1,000 card payment.
Authorize, then capture
You can capture right away. You can also
authorize and capture
in two steps, with the capture later. Hotels, for example, often authorize the full amount before a guest arrives and capture at checkout.
With Stripe, you set
capture_method=manual
. After authorization, the payment's status becomes
requires_capture
You can capture less than you held, and Stripe releases the rest automatically.

The hold does not last forever. Stripe says an online card authorization is usually valid for 7 days. For Visa payments that you start without the customer, the table says 5 days, and the exact window is 4 days and 18 hours.
Other payment methods have their own windows.
If the hold expires before capture, the funds are released and the payment is canceled.
On Stripe, the charge's
capture_before
field shows when the hold expires.
Build an alert for holds that are about to expire.
If you no longer want the money, cancel before capture. At Stripe, canceling costs nothing, while a refund after success might cost a fee.
3-D Secure
Sometimes the issuing bank wants proof that the real cardholder is paying. With
3-D Secure
(3DS), the bank may ask for a password, a one-time code sent to the phone, or a biometric check.
Rules in the EEA, the UK, India, Japan and Australia may require it for card payments.
On Stripe, the payment waits in the
requires_action
status until the customer finishes this step.
Settlement takes days
Capture is not cash. The money still has to travel between banks. Stripe gives settlement timing per country as "T+X" days. "T" is when the payment was confirmed or captured.

Stripe's table has an "initial settlement timing" column, which applies to your first payout. There it lists 2 business days for the United States. For India, it lists 2 business days for domestic charges and 5 for international ones.
Later payouts follow a default timing, which can differ.
Your processor and contract may differ too, so read your own terms.
Then a payout sends the money to your bank. Stripe's
payout.paid
event means the payout is
expected
to arrive. If it then fails, a
payout.failed
event comes later.
Refunds and chargebacks
A
refund
is started by you. At Stripe, you can refund part or all of a payment, but never more than the original charge.
It is not instant. Stripe says the customer sees the credit about 5 to 10 business days later, depending on the bank.
A refund can also fail, for example on a closed bank account.
A
chargeback
, also called a dispute, is started by the cardholder with their issuer. The network reverses the payment at once. Stripe then takes the amount and a dispute fee from your balance.
On Stripe, you usually have 7 to 21 days to respond, depending on the card network. If you miss the
deadline
, you lose.
If you counter the dispute, the cardholder's bank decides the outcome. Stripe says this can take up to 3 months.
So money you counted can leave your account weeks after a "successful" sale. Your
ledger
needs entries for refunds, disputes and fees, not only sales.
Webhooks: verify, then dedupe
Many results arrive later, for example when a bank confirms a payment or a customer disputes a charge. The processor tells you with a
webhook
Treat each one with care.
Verify the signature.
Without it, an attacker could send a fake "payment succeeded" event and get free goods.
Stripe signs each event with HMAC-SHA256 in the
Stripe-Signature
header. Verify it on the raw request body.
Reject old events.
The signed timestamp stops replay attacks. Stripe's libraries allow 5 minutes by default.
Dedupe.
The same event can arrive more than once. Save the event IDs you have processed and skip repeats.
This is the same idea as in
Idempotency, retries and timeouts
Do not trust order.
Events can arrive out of order. If one is missing, fetch the object from the API.
Answer fast.
Return 2xx before slow work, and process from a queue. Stripe
retries
failed deliveries for up to three days in live mode.
Reconcile with the settlement report
Webhooks can be late or lost, and your code has bugs. So once a day, compare your records with the processor's. For automatic payouts, Stripe's payout
reconciliation
report lists every payment, refund, dispute and fee inside each payout.
Match each line to your
ledger
and explain every difference. Meera's team would have seen the missing money in the first daily check.
PCI DSS scope
PCI DSS
is the security standard for anyone who stores, processes or transmits card data.
If your servers handle raw card numbers, you may face more than 300 security controls.
Most teams avoid that. They use
hosted fields
or a hosted checkout page, so the card number goes straight from the browser to the processor. It never passes through your servers.
You may still store the card brand, the last four digits and the expiry date.
Your
scope
shrinks, but you still must attest to PCI compliance every year.
Capture at once
One charge.
Refunds for items you cannot deliver. Refunds can cost fees.
Digital goods and in-stock items that ship the same day.
Authorize now, capture later
A hold, then a charge. Some statements do not show the difference.
The hold expires before capture, and the payment is canceled.
Stock checks, hotels, rentals, or a final amount that may drop.
Trust webhooks only
Nothing.
Missed or late events leave orders in the wrong state.
Never alone.
Webhooks plus daily reconciliation
Nothing.
More work for your team.
Always, for real money.
Your own card form
Your design.
Raw card data on your servers, and a much larger PCI scope.
Rarely. Only with a strong reason and a security team.
Hosted fields or checkout
The processor's fields in your page.
Less control over the look.
The default for most teams.
Simple rule:
store every payment state, verify and dedupe every webhook, and reconcile every payout.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Draw the payment
state machine
for your product, with every state and every exit, before you write code.
Ask:
"What happens if this webhook never arrives? If it arrives twice? If it arrives before the one before it?"
Store the processor's payment ID and status next to your order. Never mark an order "paid" from the browser's redirect alone.
Alert on holds close to expiry, captures that fail, refunds that fail and new disputes.
Run reconciliation daily, and give someone the job of explaining each difference.
Keep card numbers out of your systems, including logs and support tools. Use the processor's hosted fields.
"Draw the state machine of a payment in our code: every status, every event that changes it, and every place we write it. Mark any state with no exit."
"Review our webhook handler. Does it verify the signature on the raw body, reject old timestamps, dedupe by event ID and return 2xx before slow work? Show the line for each."
"Write a daily job that matches each payout line in the processor's report to our ledger. List rows found on only one side."
The handler uses the processor's official library to verify signatures. AI agents sometimes parse the JSON first, which breaks the raw-body check.
The dedupe check and the business update happen in one database
transaction
No settlement days, hold windows or fees are hard-coded from memory. They must match your processor's docs and contract.
Amounts are integers in
minor units
, as in
Money and double-entry ledgers
Test cards and test webhooks run in
CI
for capture failure, refund failure and a dispute.
No card number or CVC appears in logs, prompts or test data.
Money and double-entry ledgers
: how to record each state as balanced entries.
Idempotency, retries and timeouts
: safe retries for capture and refund calls.

q.v: Your shop authorizes a card payment at checkout and captures it when the item ships. What does authorization do?

options.v: It moves the money to your bank account.
It holds the amount on the customer's card, so you can capture it later.
It sends a payout to the merchant.

why.v: The bank checks for funds and holds the amount. The money moves only when you capture, and reaches your bank later, as a payout.

q.v: An item ships 10 days after a Visa online checkout, where the customer paid themselves. You authorized at checkout. What is the risk?

options.v: The hold may have expired, so the capture fails and the payment is canceled.

why.v: For a Visa online payment that the customer starts, Stripe lists a 7-day hold. After that the funds are released and the payment becomes canceled.

q.v: Your webhook handler gets the same payment_intent.succeeded event twice. What should it do?

options.v: Save processed event IDs and skip an event it has already handled.
Reject the second one with a 500 error.

why.v: Stripe says endpoints may receive the same event more than once, and recommends logging processed event IDs.

q.v: Why do many shops use hosted payment fields, like Stripe Elements, instead of their own card form?

options.v: Card data goes straight to the processor, so it does not pass through the shop's servers. This reduces PCI DSS work.
They remove the need for 3D Secure.

why.v: Stripe says handling raw card data can mean more than 300 PCI DSS controls. Low-risk integrations send card data straight to Stripe.

q.v: What is the difference between a refund and a chargeback?

options.v: You start a refund. A chargeback starts when the cardholder disputes the payment with their card issuer.
A chargeback is a refund made in under a day.

why.v: A dispute starts with the cardholder and their issuer. At Stripe, the payment amount and a dispute fee leave your balance before the bank decides who is right.
